questions.q: In a customer churn dataset with columns tenure_months, support_calls, plan, and churned, which column is the label?
questions.explain: The label is the column holding the answer the model is trying to predict — here, whether the customer actually churned.

options: A list of every label in the dataset
One row's full set of feature values
A chart of the model's accuracy over time
questions.explain: A feature vector is simply one example's row of feature values — its full description, minus the label.

questions.q: In the near-universal `X`/`y` convention, what does `X` represent?
options: A 2-D table of every row's feature columns
questions.explain: By convention, X holds the 2-D table of feature columns (one row per example, one column per feature), while y holds the 1-D column of labels.

questions.q: Why doesn't inference-time input include a label?
options: Labels are only used for categorical features, never numeric ones
Inference always uses a different feature set than training
The whole point of inference is to predict an outcome you don't already know, so there's no known answer to attach
Labels are removed for data privacy reasons
questions.explain: You only know the label for historical, already-resolved examples (which is why those can be used for training). For a brand-new case, the label is exactly what you're trying to predict — it can't already be known.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a categorical feature?
questions.explain: A categorical feature takes values from a fixed set of named options, like a plan type, rather than a continuous or countable number.
